newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spaniards mount more protests over ETA killing.
newsitem.headline: Spaniards mount more protests over ETA killing.

text.p: After enduring nearly three decades of Basque separatist violence, Spaniards have united in an unprecedented national outcry against the killing of a kidnapped politician.

Mass demonstrations and work stoppages were planned throughout the country for Monday, when 29-year-old Miguel Angel Blanco -- a low-ranking member of Spain's ruling party who died of gunshot wounds to the head -- was to be buried.

With emotions running high, officials appealed for calm, and police beefed up security around the offices of Herri Batasuna, the political arm of the Basque ETA rebel movement, to prevent a repeat of attacks on Sunday by angry protesters.

The Pope denounced Blanco's killing as "an act of blood". French President Jacques Chirac called it "cowardly". Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro said it "offends the conscience of the whole civil world".
But the sense of outrage was greatest in Spain, where ETA's targetting of an innocent victim was seen as a sign of increasing desperation.
"We have known the inhuman cruelty of ETA, but we would never have believed they would sink to this level of degradation," Basque leaders said in a statement after an urgent meeting.

Blanco, a Basque town councillor, was found on Saturday bound and bloodied, two bullets lodged in his brain, two days after ETA guerrillas kidnapped him. Rebels had threatened to kill him unless 500 ETA inmates were moved to prisons in the autonomous Basque region by 4 p.m. on Saturday.
He slipped into a coma and died early Sunday in a hospital in the Basque city of San Sebastian.
His casket was taken to a chapel in his hometown of Ermua, where thousands of mourners filed past late into the night.

Appearing atop a balcony at city hall, Blanco's family members clasped hands and wept while thousands of sympathisers chanted "ETA, enough. We want peace." Overcome with grief, Blanco's mother collapsed in the arms of relatives.
Blanco was to be buried on Monday with Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and Crown Prince Felipe among mourners.
Hundreds of thousands returned to the streets on Sunday to protest the killing after mass demonstrations on Saturday that attracted over a million people.
The largest gatherings -- in Madrid and the Basque cities of Bilbao, San Sebastian and Vitoria -- were peaceful.

But in Pamplona, where Spain's famous bull-running festival was suspended for a day in solidarity with Blanco's family, dozens of angry protesters clashed with ETA supporters outside the offices of the group's political wing.
Police in riot gear sprayed teargas and swung batons to restore order. Eighteen people were injured.

ETA attacks have provoked public outrage before. The group has killed 800 people in its 29-year struggle for an independent homeland. But it was the death sentence passed against such an ordinary person that cut to the heart of Spanish society.
"Miguel could have been any one of us. That's why it hurts," said one protester in Bilbao.

Basque leaders asked for an hour-long work stoppage from noon on Monday in the Basque region to express "indignation" at the killing. Spain's leading unions called on workers across the country to stop at noon and observe 10 minutes of silence.

Basque leaders and a senior official of Aznar's centre-right Popular Party called for the isolation of Herri Batasuna, which holds seats in the Basque and Navarre regional parliaments and the national congress.
But in a statement issued on Sunday night, Herri Batasuna complained that the campaign against it was tantamount to political "lynching".
At several Spanish prisons, ETA inmates were reportedly separated from the main prison population to prevent them from being targeted for attacks.
The Spanish government condemned the shooting on Saturday but made no official comment on Sunday after Blanco's death. Aznar was due to hold a news conference in Madrid on Monday morning.

Blanco was the 10th person killed by ETA so far this year. The group had kidnapped 77 people in its history and set deadlines to execute hostages only twice before. In both cases, the threat was carried out.
